title: America's Top Trade Negotiator Is Coming to India. A Deal Could Land by Mid-July.
excerpt: USTR Jamieson Greer will visit New Delhi after the G7 Summit to advance a bilateral trade agreement — but dead Indian sailors in the Gulf have added a volatile new dimension to the talks.
body:
# America's Top Trade Negotiator Is Coming to India. A Deal Could Land by Mid-July.

Washington's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, will fly to India the week after the G7 Summit to advance talks on a bilateral trade agreement, a senior U.S. administration official confirmed on Saturday. The announcement signals that despite months of tariff threats, forced-labour investigations, and diplomatic friction over dead Indian sailors in the Gulf, both sides believe a deal is still within reach.

The official said trade would feature prominently when President Joe Biden meets Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the G7 in Évian on June 17, but cautioned that no agreement would be finalized at the summit itself. "President Biden's approach always is we won't have a deal unless it's a very good deal," the official said. "We think a very good deal is possible."

The Greer visit would follow four days of technical-level trade talks that concluded in New Delhi earlier this month, which India's Commerce Ministry described as having been conducted in "a spirit of cooperation and pragmatism." Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has said the first tranche of a bilateral trade agreement could be concluded by mid-July. "We are optimistic about reaching a mutually beneficial agreement that will enhance our economic ties," Goyal stated, emphasizing the importance of the trade relationship for both nations.

The contours of a deal have been taking shape since February, when the two sides reached a framework under which the U.S. agreed to reduce its reciprocal tariff on India from 25 percent to 18 percent, while India committed to reducing tariffs and non-tariff barriers on American goods. But the landscape shifted dramatically in April when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Biden's broad tariff measures in a 6-3 ruling, holding that he had exceeded his authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

That ruling has not killed the tariff agenda — it has redirected it. Washington has since launched two Section 301 investigations against India, alleging surplus manufacturing capacity in textiles and steel, and the use of forced labour in supply chains. India has flatly rejected both charges. "This country has a hot climate, tropical climate. We wear cotton. How do we have overcapacity?" said Amitabh Kumar, India's additional trade secretary, in a pointed rebuttal. He further added, "We are committed to fair trade practices and will not accept unfounded allegations."

The U.S. has also proposed an additional 12.5 percent tariff on imports from India linked to the forced-labour probe — a charge India views as a negotiating lever rather than a genuine policy concern. New Delhi is pushing back by demanding preferential tariff treatment versus competitors, a concession Washington has so far been reluctant to extend.

The stakes are considerable. Bilateral goods trade between the two countries stood at roughly $130 billion in the year to March 2023, with India running a $42 billion surplus. The U.S. wants India to buy more American energy, agricultural products, and defense equipment. India wants its IT services, pharmaceuticals, and manufactured goods to face fewer barriers. This trade relationship is particularly significant for the Indian diaspora, as it not only impacts remittances but also strengthens family ties and professional opportunities for Indians living abroad. Many NRIs rely on the stability of this trade relationship to maintain their connections with family back home, and a successful deal could enhance their ability to support loved ones through increased economic opportunities.

But trade is no longer the only item on the agenda. The killing of three Indian seafarers by U.S. Navy strikes in the Gulf of Oman this week has injected a sharp edge into what was already a complicated relationship. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar lodged a formal protest with Secretary of State Antony Blinken, calling the strikes on commercial shipping "not justified." Biden, in a social media post, separately accused Iran of launching drone attacks against Indian ships — placing India squarely in the crossfire of a conflict it played no part in starting.

The Modi-Biden bilateral on June 17 will now carry the weight of both files: trade and maritime security. For India, the ideal outcome would be a tariff concession paired with an American commitment to protect, not target, Indian merchant vessels. For Biden, a trade deal with the world's fastest-growing major economy would be a domestic win ahead of a turbulent political season.

Greer's post-G7 trip to New Delhi suggests the White House believes the political will exists to close the gap. Whether it can survive the distrust building over dead sailors in the Strait of Hormuz is another question entirely. As the negotiations unfold, the Indian diaspora will be watching closely, as the outcomes could significantly affect their economic prospects and ties to their homeland. The implications of these discussions extend beyond borders, influencing the lives of millions of Indians abroad who are eager for a stable and prosperous relationship between the U.S. and India.

nri_angle: A U.S.-India trade deal directly affects NRIs through tariff structures on remitted goods, pharmaceutical pricing, IT services market access, and the broader economic relationship that shapes visa and immigration policy.
author: Diaspora Desk
